dutch_ocr:
't als de „Nachtschool" van zich afgeschoven, ja gestooten. Men had
het onder de naamhebbende theologen te druk met de echtheid van de
Bijbelboeken en met kritische schifting van den heiligen tekst. De eigen-
lijke dogmatiek gleed onder de paperassen weg, en het was metterdaad
een ontdekking voor mij, toen ik in 1873, met wijlen Ds. Gewin naar
een antiquaar te Leiden getogen, daar heel een bibliotheek vond en aan-
kocht, waaruit het oude Calvinisme nog als met graftaal mij toesprak.
Zoo kwam ik tot de oude litteratuur, en vooral door Dibbets tot de erven
der geestelijke nalatenschap. Dit bewoog mij toen om in de Gemeene
Gratie de oude Calvinistische politiek weer aan onzen zoo anders ge-
worden tijd aan te passen. Daaraan dankte toen de Gereformeerde theo-
logie van het Neo-Calvinisme haar opkomen; en weer als vanouds staat
thans deze Gereformeerde Theologie als een kracht in 't land, beide én in
de Hervormde Kerk, die nog altoos tast naar hygiënisch herstel, én in de
Gereformeerde Kerken, die met haar braken.

Doch vanzelf kon 't hierbij niet blijven. Zooals Paulus het in Corinthe
en Rome vond, en onze Calvinisten het in de 16e eeuw voelden, Religie en
Politiek waren nu eenmaal niet van elkander af te scheiden. Dit gold in
Paulus' dagen, het was niet anders in de dagen der Calvinisten ge-
weest, en even als toen, zoo deed 't zich ook nu voor: „Gij ziet uwe
roeping, broeders, dat gij niet vele wijzen zijt, niet vele machtigen, niet vele
edelen". Prins Willem van Oranje klaagde het zoo diep uit zijn teleurge-
steld hart, dat het Verbond der Edelen hem geen steun had geboden, terwijl
schier enkel uit de „kleyne luyden" hem verwinnende kracht was toegevloeid.
En ook nu weer liet schier al wat hoog in naam en macht was, Groen
van Prinsterer alleen staan, en was het in hoofdzaak de kleine burger
en de kloeke landman, bij wie zijn oproeping nog gehoor vond. In de dagen
van Paulus' apostolaat was het de „wetenschap" der Grieksche en Ro-
meinsche wijsgeeren, die de leiding der geesten in handen hield, en die
minachtend, ja verachtend, op wat de man van Tarsen schreef, neerzag.
Leg tegenover deze minachting dier toenmalige „wetenschap" nu enkel den
brief aan de Romeinen, een boekske, zoo ge het apart uitgaaft, van nog niet
één vel druks, en vraag u af, of niet de levens- en wereldbeschouwing die
Paulus hierin ten beste gaf, in diepte van opvatting en in bestraling met
hooger licht, alwat toen Rome's en Griekenland's intellectueelen ora-
kelden, geheel in de schaduw stelt. Er was daarom niets vreemds in, dat een
pittige kern als oudtijds in de eerste Christenen, en vóór nu drie eeuwen
in de Calvinisten optrad, ook nu weer van zich hooren liet, en degelijk wist
critical_translation:
't as the "Night School" [Dutch: Nachtschool] pushed away from itself, yea, thrust away. One was, among the named theologians [Dutch: naamhebbende theologen], too busy with the authenticity of the Biblical books [Dutch: Bijbelboeken] and with critical sifting of the holy text. The actual dogmatics [Dutch: dogmatiek] slipped away among the papers, and it was indeed a discovery for me, when in 1873, with the late Rev. [Dutch: Ds.] Gewin, having journeyed to an antiquarian in Leiden [Dutch: Leiden], I found and purchased there an entire library, from which the old Calvinism [Dutch: Calvinisme] still spoke to me as with sepulchral language [Dutch: graftaal]. Thus I came to the old literature, and especially through Dibbets [Dutch: Dibbets] to the heirs of the spiritual legacy [Dutch: geestelijke nalatenschap]. This then moved me to adapt the old Calvinistic politics [Dutch: Calvinistische politiek] in Common Grace [Dutch: Gemeene Gratie] again to our time, which had become so different. To this then the Reformed theology [Dutch: Gereformeerde theologie] of Neo-Calvinism [Dutch: Neo-Calvinisme] owed its rise; and again as of old, this Reformed Theology [Dutch: Gereformeerde Theologie] now stands as a power in the land, both in the Reformed Church [Dutch: Hervormde Kerk], which still always gropes for hygienic recovery [Dutch: hygiënisch herstel], and in the Reformed Churches [Dutch: Gereformeerde Kerken], which break forth with it [note: or: emerge with it].

But of itself it could not remain thus. As Paul [Dutch: Paulus] found it in Corinth [Dutch: Corinthe] and Rome [Dutch: Rome], and our Calvinists [Dutch: Calvinisten] felt it in the 16th century, Religion [Dutch: Religie] and Politics [Dutch: Politiek] were simply not to be separated from one another. This held true in Paul's [Dutch: Paulus'] days, it was no different in the days of the Calvinists [Dutch: Calvinisten], and just as then, so it presented itself now also: "Ye see your calling, brethren, that ye are not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble." Prince William of Orange [Dutch: Prins Willem van Oranje] complained so deeply from his disappointed heart, that the Covenant of Nobles [Dutch: Verbond der Edelen] had offered him no support, whilst almost solely from the "common people" [Dutch: kleyne luyden] conquering strength [note: or: victorious power] had flowed to him. And also now again, almost all that was high in name and power, left Groen van Prinsterer [Dutch: Groen van Prinsterer] standing alone, and it was mainly the small burgher and the sturdy farmer, with whom his appeal still found a hearing. In the days of Paul's [Dutch: Paulus'] apostolate [Dutch: apostolaat] it was the "science" [Dutch: wetenschap] of the Greek and Roman philosophers [Dutch: wijsgeeren], which held the guidance of spirits [Dutch: geesten] in its hands, and which looked down disdainfully, yea contemptuously, upon what the man of Tarsus [Dutch: Tarsen] wrote. Set against this disdain of that then-current "science" [Dutch: wetenschap] now only the epistle to the Romans [Dutch: Romeinen], a small book, if you publish it separately, of not yet one sheet of print [Dutch: vel druks], and ask yourself, whether not the life- and worldview [Dutch: levens- en wereldbeschouwing] that Paul [Dutch: Paulus] therein gave his best, in depth of conception and in illumination with higher light, entirely overshadows all that Rome's and Greece's intellectuals [Dutch: intellectueelen] then oracled. There was therefore nothing strange in, that a vigorous core as of old in the first Christians [Dutch: Christenen], and before now three centuries in the Calvinists [Dutch: Calvinisten] appeared, also now again made itself heard, and knew thoroughly [note: or: knew well]

it had pushed away, yea, thrust away, as the 'Night School'. Among the named theologians, one was too preoccupied with the authenticity of the Biblical books and with the critical sifting of the sacred text. Actual dogmatics, however, slipped away amidst the papers; and it was indeed a profound discovery for me when, in 1873, having journeyed with the late Rev. Gewin to an antiquarian in Leiden, I there found and purchased an entire library, from which the old Calvinism still spoke to me as with sepulchral language. Thus came I to the ancient literature, and especially through Dibbets, to the inheritors of that spiritual legacy. This, then, moved me to adapt the old Calvinistic politics, rooted in Common Grace, once more to our age, which had become so profoundly altered. Hence, to this did the Reformed theology of Neo-Calvinism owe its emergence; and again, as of old, this Reformed Theology now stands as a potent force in the land, both within the Hervormde Kerk, which still ever gropes for hygienic recovery, and within the Gereformeerde Kerken, which emerge with it.

Nevertheless, of itself, it could not remain thus. For as Paul found it in Corinth and Rome, and our Calvinists perceived it in the sixteenth century, Religion and Politics were simply inseparable. This held true in Paul's day, it had been no different in the days of the Calvinists, and even as then, so it presented itself now: 'Ye see your calling, brethren, that ye are not many wise, not many mighty, not many noble.' Prince William of Orange lamented so deeply from his disappointed heart that the Covenant of Nobles had offered him no support, whilst almost solely from the 'common people' had conquering strength flowed unto him. And even now again, almost all that was high in name and power left Groen van Prinsterer standing alone, and it was chiefly the small burgher and the sturdy farmer with whom his appeal still found a hearing. In the days of Paul's apostolate, it was the 'science' of the Greek and Roman philosophers that held the guidance of spirits, and which looked down disdainfully, yea, contemptuously, upon what the man of Tarsus wrote. Now, set against this disdain of that then-current 'science' merely the Epistle to the Romans—a small book, if one were to publish it separately, of not yet one sheet of print—and ask yourselves whether the life- and worldview Paul therein presented, in its depth of conception and its illumination with a higher light, does not entirely overshadow all that Rome's and Greece's intellectuals then oracled. There was, therefore, nothing strange in the fact that a vigorous core, as of old in the first Christians and three centuries prior in the Calvinists, should now again make itself heard, and indeed knew thoroughly
